The highlight of winter for gardeners is the trip to the mailbox to see what thrills await. The seed catalogs arrive, bringing the promise of warmth and new life!

So many beautiful colors and luscious descriptions of both food and flower. Depending on your degree of addiction, it can be downright intoxicating.

However, even some hard-core gardeners (myself definitely included) can find that the excitement of those gorgeous pictures fades when the humidity and weeds and pests come calling in the heat of summer. So in an effort to help you maintain the motivation and excitement you have right now, consider growing some unusual and less common vegetables this year.

A bonus is that most of the seed varieties I’m suggesting are heirlooms that not only have resistance to many pests and diseases, but typically offer ease of growing and high yields. Finally, all veggies discussed can be direct-seeded.

One of my all-time favorites is the Dragon Tongue bean, a lovely (and large!) alternative to boring ol’ green beans. This is a Dutch heirloom and sports light yellow 7” pods with pretty purple streaks.

If you have the space, consider growing melons. Although not quite old enough to be considered a true heirloom, the flesh of the hefty Orangeglo will be a stunner at your summer picnics. Growing up to 25 pounds, the flesh is deep orange and quite sweet, and the vines tend to be hearty and resistant to pests and common diseases.

Moon and Stars is another very sweet variety, albeit with the typical pink flesh. These melons average 10 pounds and are named for the large yellow spot (moon) accompanied by many smaller “stars” of yellow on the dark green skin. A final unusual watermelon to consider adding to your summer garden is Cream of Saskatchewan. Although it sports a more typical green striped skin, this heirloom variety has sweet-tasting, creamy white flesh.

A quite unusual and fun alternative to the typical garden cucumber is the Lemon Cucumber. This variety dates back to the 1890s, and one look explains the name: this cuke is the size, shape and color of a lemon and has a mild taste. This variety is also a darling of epicurean discussions online.

Let’s talk summer squash. Costada Romanesca is deeply ribbed, with a gray-green skin with paler green flecks. It actually yields less than traditional summer squash, (one veggie where this could be considered a plus!) and it has better flavor: nutty with a nice texture, both raw or cooked.

Add some garden color with Saffron squash, a slightly warty crookneck that grows to 4-6” and is a lovely pale to golden yellow color. The prolific yield is more typical of summer squash. Another option is Benning’s Green Tint, an heirloom patty-pan squash with fruits that are creamy white and 3-4 inches in diameter when mature.

You can easily find sources online for these seeds, but my favorite vendors include Baker Creek, Southern Exposure, Fedco and Johnny’s Seeds.
